summary: Specifies the algorithms, key formats, key sizes, and signature formats for BGPsec. It updates RFC 7935 and obsoletes RFC 8208, adding Algorithm IDs for documentation and experimentation. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: BGPsec signs route announcements. This document lists which signing methods and key shapes to use so everyone does it the same way.

subtitle: The signing algorithm, key format and signature format that BGPsec routers use, plus the reserved ranges of algorithm IDs.

tldr.problem: BGPsec routers sign and verify route announcements, and everyone must agree on exactly which algorithm, key format and signature format to use, and how to label them.
tldr.mechanism: Algorithm ID 0x01 means ECDSA with curve P-256 and SHA-256. The RFC fixes the public key encoding and signature format, and splits the one-octet ID space into reserved, assigned, unassigned, experimentation and documentation ranges.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8208 and updates RFC 7935, adding experimentation and documentation IDs and correcting the unassigned range. It also gives worked example BGPsec UPDATE messages.

today: RFC 8608 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2019. It obsoletes RFC 8208 and updates RFC 7935, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This Document Specifies
sections.content:
RFC 8608 specifies the digital signature algorithm and parameters, the hash algorithm and parameters, the assignment and classification of algorithm identifiers, the public and private key formats, and the signature formats. They are used by Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) Certification Authorities and by BGPsec speakers, meaning routers.

CAs use the algorithms when processing requests for BGPsec Router Certificates (RFC 8209). Routers use them when requesting those certificates and when signing and verifying BGPsec UPDATE messages (RFC 8205).

The RFC updates RFC 7935 in three ways: a different algorithm for BGPsec certificate requests, a different Subject Public Key Info format for BGPsec certificates, and different signature formats for BGPsec signatures. BGPsec certificates are told apart from other RPKI certificates by the BGPsec Extended Key Usage from RFC 8209. BGPsec uses a different algorithm from the rest of the RPKI to get similar security with smaller keys, which makes certificates, signatures and PDUs smaller.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone who signs and checks route announcements has to use the same kind of signature. This document picks one and writes down how it must look.

sections.title: Algorithm IDs and the ECDSA P-256 Suite
sections.content:
A BGPsec UPDATE message names its algorithm in the Algorithm Suite Identifier field (the algorithm ID) of each Signature_Block. The RFC defines five types of ID:

  • Reserved: 0x00 and 0xFF. They MUST NOT appear in a Signature_Block, and a router that sees one MUST treat the UPDATE as malformed.
  • Signature: IDs for real algorithms.
  • Unassigned: free for future assignment and MUST NOT be used until assigned. A router SHOULD treat one as an unsupported algorithm.
  • Experimentation: 0xF7 to 0xFA. A router seeing one outside an experimental network SHOULD treat it as unsupported.
  • Documentation: 0xFB to 0xFE. A router SHOULD treat these as unsupported too.

The experimentation and documentation blocks exist so that tests and examples do not clash with publicly assigned IDs in deployed networks, and do not risk production routing.

The one signature algorithm defined is ID 0x01: ECDSA with curve P-256, and the hash MUST be SHA-256. Hashes are not named alone in certificates or UPDATEs. In certificate requests the ecdsa-with-SHA256 OID MUST appear in the PKCS #10 signatureAlgorithm field or the CRMF POPOSigningKey algorithm field, and in UPDATEs the ID 0x01 goes in the Algorithm Suite Identifier field.
sections.plainLanguage: Every signature carries a number saying which kind of pen was used. Number 1 is the real one. Some numbers are held back, some are for practice runs and some are for textbook examples.

sections.title: Key and Signature Formats
sections.content:
Keys and signatures on CA certificates, BGPsec Router Certificates and CRLs follow RFC 7935. The new rules cover certificate requests, router certificates and BGPsec UPDATE messages.

ECDSA private keys MUST be associated with the P-256 elliptic curve domain parameters, and the public key MUST use the uncompressed form. The public key goes in subjectPublicKeyInfo. Its algorithm field MUST use the id-ecPublicKey OID with the parameters value secp256r1, and the subjectPublicKey field MUST be encoded as an ECPoint, all as defined in RFC 5480. The private key format is left to local policy.

The certificate and CRL signature field follows Section 4 of RFC 7935, the same as other RPKI certificates. The signature field of certification requests and BGPsec UPDATE messages MUST follow Section 2.2.3 of RFC 3279.
sections.plainLanguage: The document also says how the lock and key must be shaped, and how the signature must be written down, so any router can read any other router's.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "BGPsec Algorithm Suites" registry in the RPKI group. Each one-octet identifier names the digest and signature algorithm. The single identifier from RFC 8208, for SHA-256 with ECDSA P-256, remains valid and now points to this document.

IANA changed the unassigned range from 0x2-0xEF to 0x02-0xF6, and registered the experimentation (0xF7-0xFA) and documentation (0xFB-0xFE) ranges. Future assignments use the Standards Action process of RFC 8126.
sections.plainLanguage: A public list says what each number means. This document tidied up the list and set aside some numbers for practice and for examples.

sections.title: Security and Future Algorithms
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new security considerations. Those of RFC 3279, RFC 5480, RFC 6090, RFC 7935, RFC 8209 and RFC 8205 apply, depending on whether the object is a certificate, a certification request or an UPDATE message.

It anticipates that BGPsec will need updated key sizes and other signature and hash algorithms over time, and that this profile should be updated when appropriate. The recommended transition procedures are in RFC 6916.
sections.plainLanguage: Pens get easier to fake over time, so the document expects to pick a stronger one someday, and points to the plan for switching.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
Appendix A is non-normative. It gives example BGPsec UPDATE messages, the private keys used to make them and the certificates needed to check the signatures. The topology is AS 64496, then AS 65536, then AS 65537, and AS 64496 announces the prefixes 192.0.2.0/24 and 2001:db8::/32. Both an IPv4 and an IPv6 UPDATE are shown, signed with ECDSA P-256 and algorithm ID 0x01.

To make results repeatable, ECDSA used a fixed k value taken from RFC 6979. The RFC notes that the example certificates are expired but still useful for the purposes of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The back of the document shows complete practice messages with every number filled in, so builders can check that their own gear gets the same answers.
